question: A patient with open-angle glaucoma and moderate IOP elevation is started on a prostaglandin analogue eye drop. Which mechanism accounts for IOP reduction with this drug class?

answers.text: Increased uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humour via FP receptor activation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Prostaglandin analogues (latanoprost, bimatoprost, travoprost) activate FP (prostaglandin F2α) receptors in the ciliary muscle, relaxing it and increasing uveoscleral (unconventional) aqueous outflow. They do NOT reduce aqueous production.

answers.text: Decreased aqueous humour production via beta-1 adrenoceptor blockade in the ciliary body

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Decreased aqueous production via beta-blockade describes timolol (a non-selective beta-blocker). Prostaglandin analogues work by increasing outflow, not reducing production.

answers.text: Increased trabecular (conventional) outflow via alpha-2 agonism at the trabecular meshwork

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Alpha-2 agonists (brimonidine) primarily decrease aqueous production (and have a minor effect on uveoscleral outflow). Trabecular outflow enhancement is the mechanism of pilocarpine (muscarinic agonist), not prostaglandins.

answers.text: Osmotic reduction of vitreous volume via carbonic anhydrase inhibition

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (dorzolamide, acetazolamide) decrease aqueous production by blocking carbonic anhydrase in the ciliary body epithelium — they do not work osmotically. Osmotics (mannitol, glycerol) reduce vitreous volume but are different agents entirely.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the Anti-Glaucoma Drugs block. The two ways to lower IOP are: reduce aqueous production (beta-blockers, alpha-2 agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors) or increase outflow (prostaglandins via uveoscleral; pilocarpine via trabecular).

Excellent. Prostaglandin analogues are now first-line for open-angle glaucoma because of once-daily dosing and superior efficacy. Their mechanism (uveoscleral outflow ↑) is distinct from all other anti-glaucoma drug classes.
